INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
William English, Ph.D., is a political economist
and Assistant Professor of Strategy, Economics,
Ethics, and Public Policy at the McDonough School of
Business, Georgetown University, where he has
taught since 2016. In 2021, English conducted what
was then the largest-ever nationally representative
survey of firearms owners in order to reliably estimate
details of firearms ownership and use in the United
States. In 2026, English fielded the second wave of the
National Firearms Survey, which provides the most
comprehensive and current empirical evidence
available concerning ownership and use of AR-15 and
similarly styled rifles.
The Center for Human Liberty is a nonprofit
organization dedicated to defending and advancing
individual liberty and freedom, including the rights
and liberties protected by the Constitution.
Consistent with this purpose, the Center for Human
Liberty promotes the publication of unbiased social
science research relating to  rights and society, and
thus shares English’s interest in ensuring that the
Court is presented with the most objective and
accurate social science evidence and analysis
available.

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in
part. No person other than amici or their counsel made a
monetary contribution intended to fund its preparation or
submission.

2
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
AR-15s and similarly styled semi-automatic rifles
are in common use for lawful purposes. Professor
English’s survey-based re search supplies current
empirical evidence of this and warrants reliance.
William English, 2026 National Firearms Survey:
Results from the Second Wave, Including Current
Ownership of AR-15 Style Rifles, Other “Assault
Weapons,” and Magazines that Hold More than 10
Rounds (Working Paper, Aug. 2026),
http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7347338.
The National Firearms Survey’s 2026 wave was
fielded by a professional firm to a representative
sample of over 51,000 American adults. It reliably
shows that roughly one in ten American adults
currently owns an AR-15 or similarly styled semiautomatic rifle: “25.0% of gun owners currently own
an AR-15 type rifle, 12.9% currently own other
similarly styled semi-automatic rifles, and 30.0%—
approximately 26.4 million adults—currently own at
least one firearm in one of these two categories.” 2026
Survey at 2. On average, those who report owning an
AR-15 own 1.8 such rifles; and those who report
owning other similarly styled semi-automatic rifles
own 1.7. Id. Overall, the 2026 Survey data shows
Americans having “approximately 40 million AR-15
type rifles and 20 million other similarly styled rifles
owned in total.” Id. at 2.

3
Ordinary lawful ownership purposes dominate.
Those who own these rifles indicate that they sought
them for a range of ordinary lawful purposes,
including target shooting, hunting, competition, the
prevention of animal attacks, and defense both at
home and elsewhere. 83.0% of owners specifically
report a defensive purpose as a reason for owning
such rifles. Id. at 41.
To ensure that it accurately measured firearms
ownership and use rates, the National Firearms
Survey’s 2026 wave incorporated a number of
methodological advances. The size of the sample was
unusually large. It reached a representative national
set of 51,398 U.S. adults to identify 16,688 internallyvalidated gun owners, making it among the largest
surveys of firearms owners ever conducted. Reliability
was further enhanced by asking about current rather
than lifetime ownership, instructing respondents to
count only firearms that they personally own, and
asking about AR-15 type rifles separately from other
similarly styled rifles. These refinements responded
directly to scholarly discussion of the survey’s first
wave. The 2026 Survey’s results are robust to various
alternative weighting schemes, all of which are
reported in the survey report.
The survey’s 32.7% overall individual firearms
ownership rate aligns with other recent national
surveys. Pew found an ownership rate of 32% in 2023,

4
and Gallup found an ownership rate of 34% in 2024,
indicating a slight increase from the 31.9% rate
documented in the first wave. Id. at 11; see Katherine
Schaeffer, Key Facts About Americans and Guns (Pew
Rsch. Ctr. 2024); Gallup, Guns, Gallup Historical
Trends, https://news.gallup.com/poll/1645/guns.aspx.
Reliability is further enhanced by the 2026
Survey’s accordance with manufacturing data. The
first wave of the National Firearms Survey found in
2021 that 30.2% of gun owners had owned an AR-15
or similarly styled rifle at some point. The second
wave, conducted five years later, asking the narrower
question of current ownership, finds that 30.0% of gun
owners currently own such rifles (approximately 26.4
million adults). This finding aligns with
manufacturing data that indicates that millions of
these rifles have continued to enter the U.S. market
in recent years, which is unsurprising given that this
Court itself has described the AR-15 as “the most
popular rifle in the country.” Smith & Wesson Brands,
Inc. v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos , 605 U.S. 280, 297
(2025).
Tens of millions of ordinary, law-abiding
Americans currently own AR-15 type and similarly
styled rifles, overwhelmingly for lawful purposes.
Such arms are thus in “common use” under any
standard this Court has articulated, and the
judgments below should be reversed.

5
ARGUMENT
This Court’s precedent protects arms that are “in
common use” for “lawful purposes like self-defense.”
District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 624, 627
(2008). Whatever the standard’s outer boundaries
may be, it raises two basic fact questions: how many
Americans possess the arms, and for what purposes?
The 2026 National Firearms Survey provides
direct, current, and comprehensive answers to both
the possession and purpose questions. As to
commonality, the evidence leaves little room for
argument. Justice Alito treated stun guns as arms in
common use because hundreds of thousands had been
lawfully sold in 45 States. Caetano v. Massachusetts,
577 U.S. 411, 420 (2016) (Alito, J., concurring in the
judgment). Both halves of that showing are stronger
here. More than 26 million American adults own the
rifles banned here, and 41 States permit them. As to
purpose, this Court saw more than thirty years ago
that AR-15 possession “traditionally ha[s] been widely
accepted as lawful,” Staples v. United States, 511 U.S.
600, 612 (1994).  So too no w as well, not just as a
matter of judicial inference, but as a matter of
surveyed fact. These rifles are commonly possessed
for ordinary lawful purposes.
I. The 2026 National Firearms Survey shows
that AR-15-type and similarly styled
semiautomatic rifles are in common use
for lawful purposes.

6
A. The results of the nationally
representative 2026 English survey.
The 2026 National Firearms Survey provides the
most comprehensive assessment of firearms
ownership and use patterns in America to date. To do
so most reliably, the 2026 Survey used a uniquely
large and representative sampling of adult firearms
owners. It was fielded by the professional survey
company Centiment to a representative national
sample of 51,398 U.S. residents aged 18 and over in
the summer of 2026. It identified 16,688 internally
validated gun owners who answered in-depth
questions concerning their ownership and use of
firearms. 2026 Survey at 1–2.
A conservative approach to data integrity was
used. Respondents were counted as gun owners only
if they both indicated firearm ownership on an initial
screening question and subsequently reported a
positive number of rifles, shotguns, or handguns that
they personally own in a detailed count of firearm
types that required a response. This two-stage
validation rule guards agai nst misclicks, careless
responses, and insincere respondents. Id. at 5. All gun
owners were asked:
Some have argued that few gun owners actually
want or use guns that are commonly classified
as “assault weapons.” Do you currently own an
AR-15 or similarly styled rifle? You can include
any rifles of this style that have been modified
or moved to be compliant with local law.
However, only count rifles that you personally

7
own, not rifles that other family members may
own. Answering this will help us establish how
popular these types of firearms are.
Id. at 37, 63. Respondents could indicate, separately
or together, that they own “one or more AR-15 type
rifles” and that they own “other similarly styled semiautomatic rifles with a pistol grip,” in each case
entering the number owned. Id. at 37, 63.
Those sound methodologies yielded clear results.
25.0% of validated gun owners (95% CI 24.4%–25.7%)
report currently owning one or more AR-15 type rifles,
and 12.9% (95% CI 12.4%–13.4%) report currently
owning other similarly styled semi-automatic rifles,
with 7.9% owning both types. Overall, 30.0% of gun
owners (95% CI 29.3%–30.7%) currently own at least
one rifle in one of these categories. Extrapolated to the
population, that would mean approximately 22.1
million adults currently own an AR-15 type rifle, and
approximately 26.4 million adults currently own a
rifle of the type commonly cl assified as an “assault
weapon.” Id. at 37–38. Together, one out of every ten
adults in the United States owns at least one of these
rifles. Id. at 37–38.
The implied stock of these rifles is correspondingly
large. Among those who currently own AR-15 type
rifles, the average owner reports owning 1.8 such
rifles, and among those who own other similarly
styled rifles, the average owner reports owning 1.7.
Applying a conservative counting rule that excludes
both outlier responses and responses inconsistent
with the total number of rifles each respondent

8
separately reported owning, the survey estimates that
approximately 40 million AR-15 type rifles and 20
million other similarly styled semi-automatic rifles
are currently owned by American gun owners. Id. at
39–40.
That estimate closely aligns with reports based on
the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and
Explosives’ Annual Firearms Manufacturing and
Export Reports, which place the number of AR-15
styled rifles produced  for the American market
between 1990 and 2023 at about 32 million. NSSF,
NSSF Releases Most Recent Firearm Production
Figures (Jan. 15, 2026). In recent years the annual
number of such firearms entering the market has
averaged more than 2.5 million, so a continuation of
these trends would imply approximately 39.5 million
such rifles entering the market from 1990 through
2026, or slightly fewer if recent sales trends softened.
Moreover, these figures do not include the sizable
number of rifles commonly classified as “assault
weapons” that were produced before 1990. 2026
Survey at 40.
Ownership of these rifles is geographically and
demographically broad. Validated gun owners in
every state and the District of Columbia report
currently owning them, including in the jurisdictions
whose laws are at issue in these cases: among gun
owners, 29.9% in Illinois and 24.2% in Connecticut
currently own an AR-15 or similarly styled rifle, as do
29.9% in California, 31.0% in New York, 28.5% in New

9
Jersey, and 28.3% in Massachusetts. Id. at 43.2  The
challenged laws are outliers. The ownership they
target is not.
Ownership is also common across demographic
groups. 36.4% of Black gun owners, 38.2% of Hispanic
gun owners, 30.7% of Asian gun owners, and 21.3% of
female gun owners currently own such a rifle. Id. at
42. These are ordinary firearms chosen by a broad
cross-section of American society.
B. Owners overwhelmingly possess
these rifles for lawful purposes,
including self-defense.
When owners were asked the purposes for which
they own these rifles, they indicated the following
answers at the following rates: home defense (77.7%),
recreational target shooting (65.1%), hunting (50.2%),
defense outside the home (41.1%), prevention of
animal attacks (33.8%), competitive shooting sports
(25.9%), and other (2.8%). Taking home defense and
defense outside the home together, 83.0% of owners
cite a defensive purpose for owning these rifles. About
half also report hunting as a purpose for owning these
rifles. 2026 Survey at 41.
There are many reasons why AR-15 and similarly
styled rifles would be popular for these purposes. In

2 Note that these estimates may include versions of these
firearms that have been modified to be compliant with local law
and firearms that residents of these states keep in other states.

10
terms of ballistic performance, so-called “assault
weapons” are among the least powerful centerfire
rifles in common use.
The rifle calibers that have been most popular for
hunting big game over the last century, such as .270
Winchester, .30-06, .45-70, and .308, all generate
significantly higher muzzle energy than the .223
cartridge fired by the typical AR-15. See E. Gregory
Wallace, “Assault Weapon” Lethality, 88 Tenn. L. Rev.
1, 44–45 (2020). The .30-06 dates to 1906 and
appeared in commercial sporting rifles by 1908—
decades before the AR-15. Yet it fires a larger bullet
with substantially greater muzzle energy.
What distinguishes AR-15 and similarly styled
rifles is not their unusual power but rather a
combination of attractive features, including their
light weight, modularity, ergonomics, and low recoil.
Given these features, it is no surprise that these
firearms have consistently been among the most
popular and best-selling long guns in America.
The defensive purposes that owners cite
correspond to real concerns and real behavior. The
2026 Survey finds that 37.6% of gun owners
(approximately 33.1 million adult Americans) have
used a firearm to defend themselves, their property, a
family member, or a member of their household. It
conservatively estimates that firearms are used
defensively approximately 2.2 million times per year,
which is within the range of “about 500,000 to more
than 3 million” annual defensive uses identified by
the National Academies’ review of this literature.

11
2026 Survey at 2, 14–16;  Nat’l Rsch. Council,
Priorities for Research to Reduce the Threat of
Firearm-Related Violence  15 (2013). Rifles were the
type of firearm respondents reported using in 16.4%
of reported defensive incidents. 2026 Survey at 16. In
most defensive incidents (76.3%) the gun is never
fired, and in 70.6% of incidents the defense was so
successful that no crime remained to be reported to
police. Id. at 14, 17. About half of defensive incidents
(50.8%) involved more than one assailant, and where
a gun was fired, multiple rounds were fired 70.4% of
the time. These are circumstances for which the
capabilities of the banned rifles bear directly on
lawful self-defense. Id. at 18, 31.
C. The 2021 Survey and independent
evidence converge on the same
conclusion.
The 2026 results replicate, with improved
measurement, the findings of the first wave of the
National Firearms Survey. Compare 2026 Survey,
with William English, 2021 National Firearms
Survey: Updated Analysis Including Types of
Firearms Owned , Georgetown McDonough Sch. of
Bus. Rsch. Paper No. 4109494 (May 13, 2022),
https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4109494. In 2021,
30.2% of gun owners reported that they had ever
owned an AR-15 or similarly styled rifle. The second
wave asked the narrower question of current,
personal ownership and found essentially the same
prevalence: 30.0%. If the first wave’s lifetime framing
had substantially overstated present ownership, the

12
current-ownership estimate would have come in well
below 30.2%. It did not. 2026 Survey at 38–39.
The 2026 Survey is not alone. It accords with many
other studied conclusions. A 2022 Washington Post–
Ipsos poll of gun owners found that 20% reported
currently owning “AR-15-style rifles, including any
semi-automatic weapon built on a common AR-
platform.” Moreover, a third of AR-15 owners
indicated that their main reason for owning such
firearms was self-defense in an open-ended response
question for which they could write anything. This
survey had a margin of sampling error of plus or
minus 2.5 percentage points, bringing the range of its
ownership estimate close to the 25% rate documented
by the 2026 National Firearms Survey. See
Washington Post–Ipsos, Poll of AR-15 Owners  (Sept.
30–Oct. 11, 2022), https://perma.cc/BYG6-HT6L. The
2026 Survey result, however, was based on a sample
about eight times larger that is statistically much
better powered, and it also  reflects four additional
years of AR-15 sales, which is consistent with the
slightly higher estimate.
The 2026 wave successfully answers a critique of
the 2021 wave. Critics of the 2021 wave treated the
gap between its estimate of “assault weapons”
ownership rates and the Washington Post–Ipsos
figure as evidence of overestimation. But the question
asked by the Washington Post–Ipsos poll was in fact
a much narrower question than the one asked by the
first wave of the National Firearms Survey, which
asked about “assault weapons” at large, specifying not

13
only AR-15s but also “similarly styled rifles.” The list
of similarly styled rifles that are commonly classified
as “assault weapons” is extensive and would include,
for example: AK-47 designs, FN FALs, M1 carbines,
M1As, HK 91/93/94s and CETME/PTR clones, SKSs,
Kel-Tec rifles, Thompsons, Ruger Mini-14/Mini-30s,
FN SCARs, and Steyr AUGs and other bullpup
designs. These rifles are likewise banned under most
“assault weapons” laws, including the laws at issue
here. It is therefore essential to measure their
popularity as well—not just that of the AR-15, which
is but one instance of the banned firearm type.
William English, A Response to Critics of the 2021
National Firearms Survey  9–10 (Working Paper No.
2024-05, Nov. 25, 2024). By measuring the two
categories separately, the second wave resolved this
debate directly: 25.0% of gun owners currently own
AR-15 type rifles specifically, while 30.0% own a rifle
in the broader class that these statutes reach. The
difference between the surveys was thus primarily a
matter of question scope rather than measurement
error. 2026 Survey at 38–39.
Independent industry data parallels the 2026
Survey results. Just like English’s work, these other
studies show that the rifles at issue have accounted
for roughly one-fifth of United States firearm sales for
more than a decade. See Br. of Pet’rs 12–13 (collecting
NSSF consumer, retailer, and production data).
The empirical record thus accords with what this
Court has already recognized. The AR-15 is “the most
popular rifle in the country” and is “widely legal and

14
bought by many ordinary consumers.” Smith &
Wesson Brands, Inc. v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos ,
605 U.S. 280, 297 (2025). “Millions of Americans” own
one. Snope v. Brown , 145 S. Ct. 1534, 1534 (2025)
(Kavanaugh, J., statement respecting denial of
certiorari). The 2026 Survey quantifies the most
recent implications of those observations.
II. The second wave was designed so that
methodological questions about the first
wave could be answered with data—and
the data vindicate the original findings.
A. The survey’s design ensures
reliable results.
Survey-based estimates of firearms ownership and
use are frequently contested. To address those
concerns, the second wave utilized several design
features to optimize the reliability of its estimates.
2026 Survey at 44. It utilized both internal
consistency checks and external reliability
benchmarks.
Every gun owner analyzed in the survey passed
through two independent affirmations of ownership:
the indirect screening question at the outset, and a
positive count of specific firearm types near the end of
the survey, after an embedded attention check.
Requiring respondents to give consistent answers in
different formats at two distantly separated points in
the survey is a powerful data-integrity check. The fact
that 98.2% of respondents who indicated owning a
firearm in the screening question also confirmed

15
positive, current, personal gun ownership counts near
the end of the survey constitutes strong evidence that
the screening question was reliable. Id.
Respondents were also required to answer the AR-
15 questions with numeric values, which prevented
skipped responses and ambiguous narrative entries.
The first wave’s transparent outlier rule was applied
unchanged. Given that the survey separately
collected each respondent’s total rifle count, this
permitted another data-integrity check, requiring
that numbers entered in the itemized AR-15 and
similar-rifle question be consistent with the total
number of rifles the respondent reported owning. This
internal consistency check makes the count estimates
conservative and may neglect AR-15 styled firearms
that are classified as pistols. Id. at 39–40, 45.
The survey’s results can also be checked against
external benchmarks and alternative analytic
choices, and they hold up under both. An external
benchmark tests a survey against an independent
measurement, thereby showing whether sampling
and weighting methods generate credible estimates
beyond the questions at issue.
Here, the survey can be tested against
independently measured rates of bicycle and firearm
ownership. The indirect screening question permits
benchmarking against non-firearm items. Under the
main weighting scheme, the survey’s bicycle
ownership estimate (53.5%) is nearly identical to
Pew’s independent 53% benchmark. Id. at 45. The
top-line firearm ownership estimate (32.7%) is nearly

16
identical to the raw, unweighted rate (33.3%), which
is a function of the sample being highly representative
and weighting having very little influence. Adding
income to the weighting scheme as a robustness test
moves the estimate up, to as much as 34.9%, rather
than down. Finally, weighting the owner subsample
through a two-step procedure leaves the AR-15
findings materially unchanged (30.0% versus 29.3%,
with implied national totals essentially identical). Id.
at 12–13, 38, 52–58. With 16,688 validated gun
owners, the second wave remains, together with the
first, among the largest surveys of firearms owners
ever conducted. The complete dataset, including the
full survey instrument, is publicly available on
Harvard’s Dataverse for independent review. Id. at 4,
45. Taken together, the two waves of these surveys
report what tens of thousands of representative U.S.
gun owners answer when asked about their
ownership and use of firearms.
B. Minor criticisms of the first wave
did not survive empirical
investigation.
Critics of the first wave raised four principal
concerns about its findings with regard to “assault
weapons.” They say first that framing questions in
terms of lifetime ownership (have you owned) could
have caused overstated current ownership. They say
second that respondents, particularly women, might
have reported firearms owned by family members or
other members of their household, rather than
personal ownership. Third, they say that asking about

17
ownership of AR-15s and other similarly styled rifles
together did not allow disaggregating the two in a
manner that could be directly compared to other
surveys. Finally, although the first wave did examine
alternative weighting schemes, there was a concern
that these results were not fully reported, even
though they had no material effect on the estimates.
Deborah Azrael et al., A Critique of Findings on Gun
Ownership, Use, and Imagined Use from the 2021
National Firearms Survey: Response to William
English, 78 SMU L. REV. 239 (2025).
The second wave was designed so that each of

Asking about current ownership addresses the
lifetime-ownership objection. The 30.2% who reported

reporting current ownership in 2026.
Explicitly asking about personal ownership
addressed the household conjecture. It is notable that
even with these clarifications in place, women
constitute 45.7% of validated gun owners, higher than
the 42.2% documented in 2021, which demonstrates
that the demographic findings of the first wave were
not artifacts of question wording. 2026 Survey at 44–
45.
The separate measurement of AR-15s and other
similarly styled rifles addresses concerns about
disaggregating these two broad types of weapons. It

also reconciles the Washington Post–Ipsos figure, as
explained above.
Finally, the survey’s weighting choices, if
anything, understate ownership. Every reasonable
alternative weighting approach moves the headline
estimates up rather than down, while owner
subsample weighting yields no substantive changes.
Id. at 52–58.
One district court, evaluating the record then
before it, questioned reliance on the first-wave
evidence. See Barnett v. Raoul, 2024 WL 4719468, at
*7 (S.D. Ill. Nov. 8, 2024). Whatever one thinks of the
minor concerns raised about the first wave, the second
wave addresses them. The survey measures current,
personal ownership. It separates the rifle categories.
It validates ownership status twice. And it reports
extensive weighting and internal consistency checks.
The earlier concerns thus do not apply to the evidence
now before the Court.
III. Compilations of criminal misuse cannot
establish that these rifles are not in
common use for lawful purposes.
A. Listing incidents of criminal
misuse does not speak to the
prevalence nor the purposes of
ownership.
The decisions below gave considerable weight to
the fact that some banned ri fles had been used in a
small number of mass shootings and other tragic

19
crimes. But criminal misuse, however unfortunate,
tells the Court nothing about common use on the scale
that matters. This is what the National Firearms
Survey aims to address by measuring how many
Americans own these rifles and documenting the
reasons they indicate for owning them.
Americans own approximately 154 million rifles of
all kinds, 2026 Survey at 27, tens of millions of which
are AR-15 type or similarly styled rifles. Yet FBI data
attributes to rifles of ever y kind an average of only
425 homicides per year over the past decade—roughly
one-sixteenth the number committed with handguns,
and fewer than the numbers committed with knives
(1,604 per year) or even with hands and feet (706 per
year). See Br. of Pet’rs 13–14. Researchers across the
policy spectrum likewise estimate that “assault
weapons” of all kinds account for less than seven
percent of gun crime. Christopher S. Koper et al.,
Criminal Use of Assault Weapons and High-Capacity
Semiautomatic Firearms , 94 J.  URBAN HEALTH 313
(2017). Arms that are owned by tens of millions of
Americans and misused by a vanishingly small
fraction cannot plausibly be characterized as
“dangerous and unusual.”
B. The claim that “assault rifles”
account for the overwhelming
share of mass-shooting deaths rests
on a demonstrable coding error.
Defenders of these bans have leaned heavily on a
false statistical claim. In defending its own rifle ban,
Maryland told the Fourth Circuit that from 1981
through 2017, “[a]ssault rifles accounted for 430 or

20
85% of the total 501 mass-shooting fatalities
reported . . . in 44 mass-shooting incidents.” Supp. Br.
of Appellees at 2, Bianchi v. Frosh, No. 21-1255 (4th
Cir. Oct. 19, 2022) (quoting Charles DiMaggio et al.,
Changes in US Mass Shooting Deaths Associated with
the 1994–2004 Federal Assault Weapons Ban:
Analysis of Open-Source Data, 86 J. TRAUMA & ACUTE
CARE SURG. 11, 12 (2019)). This claim is an artifact of
a clear coding error; when the data in question is
correctly classified, the result is nearly the opposite.
In classifying the firearms used in mass shootings,
the study’s authors coded any firearm whose opensource description included the word “semiautomatic”
as an “assault rifle.” Most of the firearms so coded
were ordinary semiautomatic pistols. For example, a
“9mm Glock semiautomatic handgun” was coded as
an “assault rifle.” Amicus English identified the error
in 2018, and the authors acknowledged their
mistaken coding approach in correspondence. A
scholar whose own work favors restrictions on these
rifles independently flagged the same problem in a
letter to the editor of the journal that published the
study. Louis Klarevas, Letter to the Editor , 86 J.
Trauma & Acute Care Surg. 926 (2019); see Charles
DiMaggio et al., Authors’ Response, 87 J.  TRAUMA &
ACUTE CARE SURG. (2019).
The authors published the list of firearms they
analyzed. Charles DiMaggio et al., Weapon Details ,
https://perma.cc/76FS-UDDM. Of the 34 incidents the
study treated as assault-ri fle shootings, 17 involved
only ordinary handguns, and three more involved
handguns together with conventional rifles or
shotguns that are not encompassed by any ban.

21
Coding the firearms properly, only 12 of the 44
incidents, or about 27%, involved an “assault rifle.”
Classifying one incident as not involving a mass
shooting at all, and thus lowering the denominator,
Klarevas arrives at an estimate of roughly 30%. In
other words, roughly three-quarters of the mass
shootings in the study’s own data did not involve an
“assault rifle” at all, which is close to the opposite of
the top-line result reported by the paper.
Independent, peer-reviewed research is consistent
with the corrected count. A 2025 study in JAMA
Network Open examining every publicly targeted fatal
mass shooting from 1966 through late 2023 found that
an “assault weapon” of any kind was present in only
29.9% of incidents, and was the only firearm present
in only 7.1%, while a handgun was present in 78.8%.
Leslie M. Barnard et al., Firearm Type and Number
of People Killed in Publicly Targeted Fatal Mass
Shooting Events , 8 JAMA Network Open e2458085
(2025). Through 2025, handguns remain the weapon
most commonly used in mass public shootings.
Rockefeller Inst. of Gov’t, Mass Shooting Factsheet
(2025), https://perma.cc/L5F3-8Q64.
C. Claims that these rifles are
uniquely dangerous do not
withstand scrutiny and could not
justify the bans in any case.
Respondents can be expected to portray AR-15s
and similarly styled rifles as a uniquely destructive
“weapon of war.” See, e.g., Supp. Br. of Appellees at 2,
Bianchi v. Frosh, No. 21-1255 (4th Cir. Oct. 19, 2022).
As explained above, see supra  Part I.B, so-called

22
“assault weapons” are among the least powerful
centerfire rifles in common use. The accusations
typically leveled at the .223-chambered AR-15, such
as that its bullets penetrate walls and inflict
devastating wounds, are even more true of most
traditional hunting rifles manufactured a century
ago. A .30-06 deer rifle fires a far larger bullet with
substantially greater muzzle energy than the typical
AR-15, see Wallace, supra, at 44–45, and no one
supposes that deer rifles may be banned on that
account.
Nor has experience shown that banning these
rifles delivers exceptional safety benefits. The
Department of Justice-funded assessment of the 1994
federal ban concluded that “we cannot clearly credit
the ban with any of the nation’s recent drop in gun
violence,” and found “no discernible reduction in the
lethality and injuriousness of gun violence” during the
ban years. Christopher S. Koper, An Updated
Assessment of the Federal Assault Weapons Ban:
Impacts on Gun Markets and Gun Violence, 1994–
2003, at 96 (2004).
Firearms homicides and mass shootings have
declined precipitously at the same time that
ownership of AR-15 and similarly styled rifles has
expanded to include nearly one out of ten U.S. adults.

that, by any measure this Court has employed, the
firearms at issue here are in common use. The
